name: Illegalism
summary: Illegalism is a current of individualist anarchism, mainly French around 1886-1914, that treated crime as revolt. Its adherents held that theft (individual reclamation), burglary, counterfeiting and violence against the bourgeoisie were legitimate ways to live free of wage labour and to strike at property, the state and law at once. They rejected the state, law, property, religion, the military and family, and other anarchists criticised them as selfish and ineffective.
scope: Illegalism as a tendency of individualist anarchism, mainly French (with Italian and Belgian links) from the mid-1880s to the First World War, defined by its practice of individual reclamation: theft, burglary, counterfeiting and swindling as anarchist revolt against property and law (Frayne; Imrie; Simons). Its figures are Clément Duval, who theorised it at his 1886 trial, Marius Jacob and his Travailleurs de la nuit, and the Bonnot Gang. Texts: Jacob's 1905 trial statement and Duval's memoir. Excludes the wider individualist anarchism of Libertad or Armand, the 1890s bomb attacks (Ravachol, Henry) as such, and anarchists who only tolerated expropriation; Jacob's 1948 doubts about illegalism are noted but are not the doctrine.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Frayne lists the military among the institutions illegalists rejected and sought to demolish.

alienated-labor.rationale: Jacob said work pleased him but he hated sweating blood and tears for a pittance and creating wealth he was denied, calling wage work 'the prostitution of work'.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Frayne and Imrie say illegalist acts were meant as exemplary invitations to revolt; Simons says Bonnot's gang held the deed itself to be the insurrection, not a way to educate the masses.

class-collaboration.rationale: Jacob told the court that those who produce everything have nothing, which can only produce antagonism between the laboring and the owning class, and he 'made war on the rich'.

clerical-rule.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of religion and the state, and Imrie reports Jacob's band robbed priests as social parasites.

conscription.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the state and of the military.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Frayne says illegalists were not opposed to rules that result from common consent but saw laws imposed without it as unwarranted authority.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the state, so state-recognised bargaining bodies are excluded.

democracy-best.rationale: Jacob scorned "your institutions" and denied anyone's right to judge him, rejecting parliamentary order.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Jacob held that every man has a right to life's banquet and that the struggle ends when 'all will belong to everyone', with labours and riches put in common.

gradual-change.rationale: Imrie says illegalists were tired of waiting for the revolution, and Hégot's circle refused to wait for the masses to evolve; they sought to live free at once.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Jacob complained that the more a man works the less he earns and the less he produces the more he benefits, calling the owning class do-nothing.

informal-organisation.rationale: Frayne's typology lists affinity groups or no organisation as the insurrectionist form of association, to which Simons' account of the gangs also points.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of religion and of law as a hurdle to freedom.

means-match-ends.rationale: Jacob condemned theft yet used it as the means of revolt against property, and Frayne notes illegalists did not prefigure the world they wanted.

military-superiority.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the military and the state.

more-religion-public.rationale: Frayne records illegalists as demolishing the established order, including a rejection of religion.

natural-rulers.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the state and of all unjustified authority.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Imrie reports that Jacob's band excluded murder except in legitimate self-defence, and Duval defended stabbing a policeman as self-defence.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Property protection by the state is just what they attacked.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Frayne quotes the illegalist maxim that the anarchist need not take the law into account, despising it in principle, and says to respect it was to submit to unwarranted authority; Jacob recognised no one's right to judge him.

one-party-rule.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the state, so a party holding exclusive rule of it is excluded.

patriotic-education.rationale: Imrie quotes the illegalist press: 'We have had enough of always sacrificing ourselves for something. The Fatherland, Society and Morality have fallen.'

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Jacob said that only the bold take hold of power and hasten to legalize their rapine, and that the social scale is dastardy above and idiocy below.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Frayne's account of the insurrectionist branch, of which the illegalist is one manifestation, says acts of violence are necessary, warranted and encouraged; Imrie calls illegalist and bomber acts a personal, violent rejection of society.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Jacob held that those who produce everything have nothing while those who produce nothing have everything, and that the wealth was created by the poor and stolen from them by the rich.

property-fundamental.rationale: Jacob called individual property 'the most unjust of all thefts' and says there are no worse thieves than landlords; Frayne records illegalism as a rejection of property.

religion-illusion.rationale: Jacob said priests promise paradise to their dupes while the state offers a piece of paper; Imrie notes the band robbed priests and left a graffito mocking God.

religious-nation.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of religion and of the state.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Jacob closed his defence with 'Revolutionary anarchist, I made my revolution', and Frayne describes illegal acts against bourgeois institutions as praised revolutionary acts.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Jacob told the court that respect for property, rooted in the people, is its best gendarme, since force alone is powerless.

self-interest-moral.rationale: A Hégot quotation in Imrie says the individual has a right to all possible well-being and must pursue it by any means; Simons notes the unions of egoists.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Frayne says illegalists saw laws as the domination of the rich over the poor, defending an elite's interests; Jacob said the powerful 'legalize their rapine' and called police the rich's valets.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the state, so a state directing investment is excluded.

state-harmful.rationale: Frayne records illegalists as challenging and demolishing the established order, including a rejection of the state; Jacob called himself a revolutionary anarchist and fought 'agents of power'.

strong-leader.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of the state, which a strong leader of it would contradict.

traditional-family.rationale: Frayne records the illegalist rejection of property, the state, religion, the military and the family.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Frayne says illegalists held laws favouring an elite to be fundamentally unjust and that breaking them was an ethical necessity.

notes: Themes searched in the four sources: property, state, law, violence, revolution, work, religion, military, nation, family, organisation. Most statements are null since the illegalists said nothing on them. The downloaded book for Jacob (d'Herbelot's Bibliothèque orientale) is a false match and is not used. Jacob's 1948 doubts about illegalism are noted by Imrie and Simons but do not change his earlier stated position.

keyFigures.role: First illegalist; theorised individual reclamation at his 1886 trial
keyFigures.quote: Illegalism may be said to have begun in 1886 with the trial of Clément Duval

keyFigures.role: Burglar-anarchist who led the Travailleurs de la nuit and defended illegalism at his 1903-1905 trial
keyFigures.quote: Arrested in 1903, the 26-year-old Jacob used his trial to defend illegalism.
